scenes.title: Where Ceibal’s blade makers found stone
scenes.body: Volcanic glass reached Ceibal from the Guatemalan highlands. In Terminal Preclassic contexts the largest share came from San Martín Jilotepeque. Shifts between nearby sources show how the making of ordinary tools depended on changing networks.
scenes.note: The window represents dated archaeological contexts and cannot locate intermediate exchanges.

scenes.title: Green obsidian in workshops and households
scenes.body: At Tlajinga in Teotihuacan, work surfaces preserve the debris of making blades. Across Mesoamerica in Tikal, objects made from the same central Mexican glass occur in several kinds of deposits. At Ceibal, tool makers mostly relied on El Chayal.
scenes.note: The lines link geological sources to finds. Similar source material can reach different communities through different people.

scenes.title: Distant stone in Honduras and Hispaniola
scenes.body: In the Cacaulapa Valley, late contexts at El Coyote contain material from the Pachuca source. At Playa Grande in Hispaniola, three tested jade celts point back to the Motagua region. One fragment could be from a ninth- or tenth-century context, though that context also has a later age.
scenes.note: The El Coyote contexts cluster near 900 CE. The Playa Grande connection carries a provisional early age and a competing 1340–1470 CE age.

scenes.title: Island households and mainland materials
scenes.body: On Isla del Tigre, people worked obsidian from both Ixtepeque and Güinope. Farther southeast on the Caribbean side of the isthmus, Sitio Drago’s pottery includes sherds that excavators compare with makers’ traditions in the Diquís. Island residents took part in several overlapping systems of exchange.
scenes.note: The Gulf of Fonseca assignments rest on geochemical tests. The Diquís link uses ceramic comparisons and remains a proposed source region.

scenes.title: Copper from two directions
scenes.body: At Mound City in Ohio, people laid copper ornaments and other pieces of metal in ceremonial deposits. Chemical comparisons link samples from the earlier Mound 8 to the Lake Superior district. In a later building context at Mound 13, southern Appalachian matches predominate.
scenes.note: The viewing year is near the boundary between approximate archaeological contexts. The separate connections represent regional assignments from a small sample.

scenes.title: From highland glass to Pacific shell
scenes.body: People at Quilcapampa and Corralones received obsidian from distant geological sources. At Omo, another kind of obsidian linked a lower valley to the Bolivian highlands. At Khoa Reef, people deposited carved Pacific shell in the waters of Lake Titicaca.
scenes.note: Chemistry identifies materials, while archaeological contexts supply dates. The straight lines connect evidence areas and leave intermediate stops unresolved.

scenes.title: Building at Chaco with mountain timber
scenes.body: Tree-ring matches indicate that builders carried many of Chaco’s early beams from the Zuni Mountains. People at Pueblo Bonito were also caring for scarlet macaws whose original stock came from lowland Mesoamerica.
scenes.note: Beams preserve an approximate sourcing phase. Bones provide direct dates for birds, whose immediate breeding source remains unresolved.

scenes.title: Cacao and scarlet macaws at Pueblo Bonito
scenes.body: Cacao left a chemical trace in pottery at Pueblo Bonito. Scarlet macaws left bones. The vessels and the birds preserve evidence of two connections to tropical Mesoamerica, each with its own dating and uncertainties.
scenes.note: The ceramic context and bone dates overlap. Their connections may have passed through different people or places.

scenes.title: Two trees moved for plazas
scenes.body: Near Cahokia, a bald cypress brought from the south stood as a marker at Mitchell. More than 1,500 kilometres away in the Southwest, a large ponderosa pine likely carried from the Chuska Mountains became part of the west plaza at Pueblo Bonito.
scenes.note: 1124 CE is the best estimate for the Mitchell tree’s felling. The Chaco tree’s arrival is less precisely dated and its particular use remains open.

scenes.title: Pots made their way to island ports
scenes.body: Northern Bali’s coastal settlements received fine Indian wares and made dishes of their own in similar forms. On Fais, a much smaller island farther east, imported pottery linked the earliest excavated communities to Yap and possibly through Yap to Palau.
scenes.note: The links follow ceramic evidence in named, dated receiving deposits. Their maps do not record intermediate ports or the arrangements by which vessels changed hands.

scenes.title: Stone moved within familiar country
scenes.body: Basalt from Peats Ridge–Popran Creek occurs in several dated layers at a shelter by the Macdonald River. On Tutuila, an artifact from Tataga-matau reached Aganoa, where the people made heavier use of a source closer to home.
scenes.note: Successive layers at Macdonald River establish repeated access to basalt. The Aganoa transfer is evidence from one middle-period piece.

scenes.title: Bowls arrived in Bali and travelled past Belitung
scenes.body: At Sembiran, Changsha sherds lay among stonework that excavators interpret as a harbour. Near Belitung, the ship that carried a much larger cargo of Changsha bowls sank with one dated bowl still aboard.
scenes.note: The Belitung range estimates one shipment. The Bali shore preserves several centuries of changing ceramic imports.

scenes.title: Two geological sources meet at Tikopia
scenes.body: Rare Tongan volcanic glass appears in Tikopia’s Tuakamali deposits. Earlier and later finds point to the much more common glass of the Banks Islands. The composition of the objects identifies two different regional connections at the same receiving island.
scenes.note: The dates bracket archaeological phases and the earliest evidence for the new source. The three Tongan pieces do not tell how often people travelled.
